evidence.title: An Optimization Approach of Container Startup Times for Time-Sensitive Embedded Systems
evidence.abstract: Containers are a lightweight virtualization method that is widely adopted in Cloud Environments, Internet of Things (IoT) and embedded devices. Apart from virtualization, containers provide an efficient way of building, storing and distributing layered filesystems for applications. This is one reason why containers became state of the art for service development, deployment and administration in IT systems. Although containers are lightweight, the image layering and container creation add overhead to the application startup time causing a cold start problem in serverless computing. Therefore, the overhead must be kept as small as possible, especially for resource-constrained devices in time-sensitive systems. We present a concept to decrease container startup times and perform analysis on a resource constrained device, a Renesas RCar H3. The study shows that using our concept, the average container startup time can be reduced by up to 64% on target hardware. Furthermore, we evaluate how the solution scales on different hardware setups and determine the impact of container configuration parameters on startup times.

evidence.title: Hybrid Solar and Kinetic Energy Harvesting System for Smart Microgrids for EV Charging With Integrated IOT
evidence.abstract: This project presents a Hybrid Solar and Kinetic Energy Harvesting System designed for efficient energy harvesting and smart microgrid management. The system integrates a 12V battery, charged via a photovoltaic (PV) cell and an energy harvesting mechanism from a speed breaker, ensuring a sustainable power supply. One 1W solar panel, each monitored by a voltage sensor, provide real-time voltage data to an Arduino UNO microcontroller. Simultaneously, the speed breaker-based energy harvester contributes additional power, monitored through a voltage sensor. To enhance system intelligence and remote accessibility, an IoT-enabled Wi-Fi module transmits real-time power data to an online monitoring platform. The system optimizes power distribution across three load stations using relay-based control, allowing dynamic load management based on power availability and demand. By integrating solar and kinetic energy sources, this project enhances energy efficiency and reliability in smart microgrid applications.

evidence.title: Oxygen redox in battery cathodes: A brief overview
evidence.abstract: The participation of oxygen or other anionic species in redox activities in cathode materials for lithium and sodium-ion battery systems is known to play a role in governing the useful capacity of these batteries. Directly probing anionic redox mechanisms is not possible, rather the computational analysis by density functional theory poses the main approach towards gleaning insights into anionic redox activity and harnessing these effects to maximize capacity in future electrode materials. Here we showcase material systems exhibiting this mechanism of ion insertion and removal, and present the key computational considerations in studying anionic redox activities in battery materials. Aided by new computationally derived understandings of the role of anionic redox in emerging battery materials, increasingly greater levels of useable capacities can be extracted through informed materials design.

evidence.title: Quantum battery with non-Hermitian charging
evidence.abstract: We propose a design of a quantum battery exploiting the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as a charger. In particular, starting with the ground or the thermal state of the interacting (non-interacting) Hamiltonian as the battery, the charging of the battery is performed via parity-time (PT)- and rotational-time (RT)-symmetric Hamiltonian to store energy. We report that such a quenching with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian leads to an enhanced power output compared to a battery with a Hermitian charger. We identify the region in the parameter space which provides the gain in performance. We also demonstrate that the improvements persist with the increase of system size for batteries with both PT- and RT-symmetric chargers. In the PT-symmetric case, although the anisotropy of the XY model does not help in the performance, we show that the XXZ model as a battery with a non-Hermitian charger performs better than that of the XX model having certain interaction strengths. We also exhibit that the advantage of non-Hermiticity remains valid even at finite temperatures in the initial states.

evidence.title: Energy Harvesting Communications Using Dual Alternating Batteries
evidence.abstract: Practical energy harvesting (EH) based communication systems typically use a battery to temporarily store the harvested energy prior to its use for communication. The batteries can be damaged when they are repeatedly charged (discharged) after being partially discharged (charged), overcharged or deeply discharged. This motivates the cycle constraint which says that a battery must be charged (discharged) only after it is sufficiently discharged (charged). We also assume Bernoulli energy arrivals, and a half-duplex constraint due to which the batteries are not charged and discharged simultaneously. In this context, we study EH communication systems with: (a) a single-battery with capacity 2B units and (b) dual-batteries, each having capacity of B units. The aim is to obtain the best possible long-term average throughputs and throughput regions in point-to-point (P2P) channels and multiple access channels (MAC), respectively. For the P2P channel, we obtain an analytical optimal solution in the single-battery case, and propose optimal and sub-optimal power allocation policies for the dual-battery case. We extend these policies to obtain achievable throughput regions in MACs by jointly allocating rates and powers. From numerical simulations, we find that the optimal throughput in the dual-battery case is significantly higher than that in the single-battery case, although the total storage capacity in both cases is 2B units. Further, in the proposed policies, the largest throughput region in the single-battery case is contained within that of the dual-battery case.

evidence.title: Characterization of a rotary piezoelectric energy harvester based on plucking excitation for knee-joint wearable applications
evidence.abstract: Wearable medical and electronic devices demand a similarly wearable electrical power supply. Human-based piezoelectric energy harvesters may be the solution, but the mismatch between the typical frequencies of human activities and the optimal operating frequencies of piezoelectric generators calls for the implementation of a frequency up-conversion technique. A rotary piezoelectric energy harvester designed to be attached to the knee-joint is here implemented and characterized. The wearable harvester is based on the plucking method of frequency up-conversion, where a piezoelectric bimorph is deflected by a plectrum and permitted to vibrate unhindered upon release. Experiments were conducted to characterize the energy produced by the rotary piezoelectric energy harvester with different electric loads and different excitation speeds, covering the range between 0.1 and 1 rev s −1 to simulate human gait speeds. The electrical loads were connected to the generator either directly or through a rectifying bridge, as would be found in most power management circuits. The focus of the paper is to study the capability of energy generation of the harvester for knee-joint wearable applications, and study the effects of the different loads and different excitation speeds. It is found that the energy harvested is around 160–490 {µJ} and strongly depends on the angular speed, the connected electric loads and also the manufacturing quality of the harvester. Statistical analysis is used to predict the potential energy production of a harvester manufactured to tighter tolerances than the one presented here

system.value: Hybrid Solar and Kinetic Energy Harvesting System for Smart Microgrids for EV Charging With Integrated IOT

abstract.value: This project presents a Hybrid Solar and Kinetic Energy Harvesting System designed for efficient energy harvesting and smart microgrid management. The system integrates a 12V battery, charged via a photovoltaic (PV) cell and an energy harvesting mechanism from a speed breaker, ensuring a sustainable power supply. One 1W solar panel, each monitored by a voltage sensor, provide real-time voltage data to an Arduino UNO microcontroller. Simultaneously, the speed breaker-based energy harvester contributes additional power, monitored through a voltage sensor. To enhance system intelligence and remote accessibility, an IoT-enabled Wi-Fi module transmits real-time power data to an online monitoring platform. The system optimizes power distribution across three load stations using relay-based control, allowing dynamic load management based on power availability and demand. By integrating solar and kinetic energy sources, this project enhances energy efficiency and reliability in smart microgrid applications.

system.value: Oxygen redox in battery cathodes: A brief overview

abstract.value: The participation of oxygen or other anionic species in redox activities in cathode materials for lithium and sodium-ion battery systems is known to play a role in governing the useful capacity of these batteries. Directly probing anionic redox mechanisms is not possible, rather the computational analysis by density functional theory poses the main approach towards gleaning insights into anionic redox activity and harnessing these effects to maximize capacity in future electrode materials. Here we showcase material systems exhibiting this mechanism of ion insertion and removal, and present the key computational considerations in studying anionic redox activities in battery materials. Aided by new computationally derived understandings of the role of anionic redox in emerging battery materials, increasingly greater levels of useable capacities can be extracted through informed materials design.

system.value: Energy Harvesting Communications Using Dual Alternating Batteries

abstract.value: Practical energy harvesting (EH) based communication systems typically use a battery to temporarily store the harvested energy prior to its use for communication. The batteries can be damaged when they are repeatedly charged (discharged) after being partially discharged (charged), overcharged or deeply discharged. This motivates the cycle constraint which says that a battery must be charged (discharged) only after it is sufficiently discharged (charged). We also assume Bernoulli energy arrivals, and a half-duplex constraint due to which the batteries are not charged and discharged simultaneously. In this context, we study EH communication systems with: (a) a single-battery with capacity 2B units and (b) dual-batteries, each having capacity of B units. The aim is to obtain the best possible long-term average throughputs and throughput regions in point-to-point (P2P) channels and multiple access channels (MAC), respectively. For the P2P channel, we obtain an analytical optimal solution in the single-battery case, and propose optimal and sub-optimal power allocation policies for the dual-battery case. We extend these policies to obtain achievable throughput regions in MACs by jointly allocating rates and powers. From numerical simulations, we find that the optimal throughput in the dual-battery case is significantly higher than that in the single-battery case, although the total storage capacity in both cases is 2B units. Further, in the proposed policies, the largest throughput region in the single-battery case is contained within that of the dual-battery case.

candidates.mechanism: Spurious module wake events cause parasitic current draw that depletes the 12V battery during extended parking, analogous to how continuous manual or conventional machine operation depletes farmer energy or fuel reserves without regeneration; the source system resolves this by integrating a renewable input (solar) and storage buffer to maintain net positive energy balance during idle/operation periods, which maps to adding an auxiliary solar charging circuit to offset parasitic drain in the automotive system.
candidates.intervention: Integrate a low-profile photovoltaic module connected via a dedicated charge controller to the 12V automotive battery, sized to generate current exceeding the maximum measured spurious wake event drain during daylight parking conditions.

constraint_set.problem_constraint: solution must preserve starting capability after extended airport parking without disabling required vehicle electrical systems
constraint_set.boundary_conditions: Vehicle must be exposed to sufficient global solar radiation for a minimum of 4 hours per day; ambient temperature must remain within the operational range of the lead-acid battery and PV module (-20°C to 60°C); parasitic drain must not exceed the maximum current output of the selected PV module under worst-case tilt angles.

candidates.predicted_effect: The net current flow into the battery during daylight parking will become positive, preventing the state-of-charge from dropping below the engine cranking threshold despite recurring spurious module wake events.
known_failure_modes: Insufficient solar irradiance during prolonged indoor or covered parking fails to offset drain
charge controller failure leads to battery overcharge or reverse current leakage
physical obstruction of the PV module reduces generation below the parasitic load threshold

candidates.testable_prediction: Under clear sky solar irradiance of at least 500 W/m², the battery terminal voltage after 72 hours of parking with active spurious wake events will remain above 12.4V, whereas a control vehicle without the PV module will drop below 11.8V.

warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. custody_records.raw_content: Containers are a lightweight virtualization method that is widely adopted in Cloud Environments, Internet of Things (IoT) and embedded devices. Apart from virtualization, containers provide an efficient way of building, storing and distributing layered filesystems for applications. This is one reason why containers became state of the art for service development, deployment and administration in IT systems. Although containers are lightweight, the image layering and container creation add overhead to the application startup time causing a cold start problem in serverless computing. Therefore, the overhead must be kept as small as possible, especially for resource-constrained devices in time-sensitive systems. We present a concept to decrease container startup times and perform analysis on a resource constrained device, a Renesas RCar H3. The study shows that using our concept, the average container startup time can be reduced by up to 64% on target hardware. Furthermore, we evaluate how the solution scales on different hardware setups and determine the impact of container configuration parameters on startup times.

custody_records.raw_content: This project presents a Hybrid Solar and Kinetic Energy Harvesting System designed for efficient energy harvesting and smart microgrid management. The system integrates a 12V battery, charged via a photovoltaic (PV) cell and an energy harvesting mechanism from a speed breaker, ensuring a sustainable power supply. One 1W solar panel, each monitored by a voltage sensor, provide real-time voltage data to an Arduino UNO microcontroller. Simultaneously, the speed breaker-based energy harvester contributes additional power, monitored through a voltage sensor. To enhance system intelligence and remote accessibility, an IoT-enabled Wi-Fi module transmits real-time power data to an online monitoring platform. The system optimizes power distribution across three load stations using relay-based control, allowing dynamic load management based on power availability and demand. By integrating solar and kinetic energy sources, this project enhances energy efficiency and reliability in smart microgrid applications.

custody_records.raw_content: The participation of oxygen or other anionic species in redox activities in cathode materials for lithium and sodium-ion battery systems is known to play a role in governing the useful capacity of these batteries. Directly probing anionic redox mechanisms is not possible, rather the computational analysis by density functional theory poses the main approach towards gleaning insights into anionic redox activity and harnessing these effects to maximize capacity in future electrode materials. Here we showcase material systems exhibiting this mechanism of ion insertion and removal, and present the key computational considerations in studying anionic redox activities in battery materials. Aided by new computationally derived understandings of the role of anionic redox in emerging battery materials, increasingly greater levels of useable capacities can be extracted through informed materials design.

custody_records.raw_content: We propose a design of a quantum battery exploiting the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as a charger. In particular, starting with the ground or the thermal state of the interacting (non-interacting) Hamiltonian as the battery, the charging of the battery is performed via parity-time (PT)- and rotational-time (RT)-symmetric Hamiltonian to store energy. We report that such a quenching with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian leads to an enhanced power output compared to a battery with a Hermitian charger. We identify the region in the parameter space which provides the gain in performance. We also demonstrate that the improvements persist with the increase of system size for batteries with both PT- and RT-symmetric chargers. In the PT-symmetric case, although the anisotropy of the XY model does not help in the performance, we show that the XXZ model as a battery with a non-Hermitian charger performs better than that of the XX model having certain interaction strengths. We also exhibit that the advantage of non-Hermiticity remains valid even at finite temperatures in the initial states.

custody_records.raw_content: Practical energy harvesting (EH) based communication systems typically use a battery to temporarily store the harvested energy prior to its use for communication. The batteries can be damaged when they are repeatedly charged (discharged) after being partially discharged (charged), overcharged or deeply discharged. This motivates the cycle constraint which says that a battery must be charged (discharged) only after it is sufficiently discharged (charged). We also assume Bernoulli energy arrivals, and a half-duplex constraint due to which the batteries are not charged and discharged simultaneously. In this context, we study EH communication systems with: (a) a single-battery with capacity 2B units and (b) dual-batteries, each having capacity of B units. The aim is to obtain the best possible long-term average throughputs and throughput regions in point-to-point (P2P) channels and multiple access channels (MAC), respectively. For the P2P channel, we obtain an analytical optimal solution in the single-battery case, and propose optimal and sub-optimal power allocation policies for the dual-battery case. We extend these policies to obtain achievable throughput regions in MACs by jointly allocating rates and powers. From numerical simulations, we find that the optimal throughput in the dual-battery case is significantly higher than that in the single-battery case, although the total storage capacity in both cases is 2B units. Further, in the proposed policies, the largest throughput region in the single-battery case is contained within that of the dual-battery case.

The electrical loads were connected to the generator either directly or through a rectifying bridge, as would be found in most power management circuits. It is found that the energy harvested is around 160–490 {µJ} and strongly depends on the angular speed, the connected electric loads and also the manufacturing quality of the harvester.
